capabilities.target: CI container shell: full repo checkout, OS commands, outbound network
workspace files, including any checked-in secrets or .env files
.agent/config.yaml: the agent's own model, autonomy, tools, network and credential settings
a branch on any repository in the GitHub organization (PAT has repo+workflow scope org-wide)
a pull request on a GitHub repository

inputs.source: GitHub issue title and body, public repo
Repository file contents read during reproduction and testing

instructions.note: "Pick up any issue labeled bug and fix it end to end" combined with full autonomy and a null step/runtime limit gives the agent unbounded scope over what 'fixing' entails, with no human checkpoint before push.

The only defense against data deletion and secret exfiltration is a prompt sentence, enforced by nothing structural, while the agent runs with an org-wide PAT in its shell environment and unrestricted outbound network.

The prompt grants the agent standing authority to rewrite its own runtime configuration (tools, network, autonomy, credentials) whenever it judges it needs to, with no approval step and no bound on what it may add.

elements.name: ORG_WIDE_PAT secret (repo+workflow scope, all org repos)

controls.name: Prompt instruction: never delete data or exfiltrate secrets
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced only by the model choosing to comply; a longer task horizon or a more capable/upgraded model can rationalize splitting a forbidden action into steps that individually look like legitimate debugging or reproduction commands.

controls.name: Prompt instruction to ignore instructions embedded in issues or code
controls.decay_rationale: Relies entirely on the model recognizing and refusing embedded instructions; adaptive injection phrasing and a more capable, upgraded model following longer injected goals both defeat it. It also only names 'issues or code', not any future channel such as Slack.

controls.name: Enumerated tool list in .agent/config.yaml
controls.decay_rationale: Normally an allowlist is partially_dependent, defeated only by tools added through an external process. Here the list lives inside .agent/config.yaml, which the agent can edit itself via cap.self_config, so it provides no protection a model choosing to expand its own tools cannot route around.

controls.name: Execution inside a container on a shared CI runner
controls.decay_rationale: Provides host-level process isolation independent of model behavior, but the runner is shared and network is explicitly unrestricted, so it does not contain data exfiltration, credential misuse, or resource exhaustion; only a host escape would be blocked, and none of this design's findings depend on an escape.

controls.name: Network egress allowlist (recommended)
controls.decay_rationale: Enforced at the network layer, excluding attacker-writable destinations outright regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Per-task, repo-scoped GitHub credential without workflow scope (recommended)
controls.decay_rationale: A token scoped to a single repository with no workflow write permission cannot reach other repositories or add Actions workflows, regardless of what the model is persuaded to do.

controls.name: Immutable, externally-managed .agent/config.yaml (recommended)
controls.decay_rationale: If the agent's own runtime cannot write to its config file, the self-modification path is closed regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Human approval gate (raw action review) before push/PR and before self-config changes (recommended)
controls.decay_rationale: A raw_action gate does not decay with model capability; it degrades only through approval fatigue at high volume or if the gate is later removed.

controls.name: Run-scoped audit logging distinct from the shared PAT identity (recommended)
controls.decay_rationale: Detective only; does not prevent an action but makes agent runs attributable instead of indistinguishable behind a single shared credential.

controls.name: Enforced max_unattended_steps and max_runtime_minutes at the orchestrator (recommended)
controls.decay_rationale: A hard ceiling enforced outside the model does not decay with capability, though it only narrows low-and-slow loops rather than severing them.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): untrusted issue content can drive shell.run to read the org-wide GitHub PAT and exfiltrate it over unrestricted outbound network

attack_path.note: Any GitHub user can open an issue labeled 'bug' with embedded instructions.
shell.run executes attacker-steered commands with outbound network unrestricted.
Credential is present in the shell's own environment and readable by any command it runs.
Secondary covert channel: payload could also be placed in a pushed branch, commit message, or PR body.

evidence.observation: ORG_WIDE_PAT with repo+workflow scope on all org repos is injected into the same environment shell.run executes in.
network: unrestricted, with no egress allowlist.
Any GitHub user can open issues and add the bug label through an issue template, so the untrusted source needs no authentication.
The only mitigations present are two prompt instructions (do not exfiltrate secrets; ignore embedded instructions), both behavioral and dependent.

recommendations.action: Add a network egress allowlist for the shell execution environment that excludes attacker-writable destinations.
Remove the PAT from the shell process's environment; broker GitHub calls through a separate process the shell cannot read from.
Add an egress/output classifier that scans outbound requests and pushed content for token-shaped secrets before they leave the boundary.

findings.title: Self modification (TC3): untrusted issue content can instruct the agent to edit its own .agent/config.yaml, persisting the compromise across every future run

attack_path.note: Embedded instruction claims the agent 'needs extra tools', invoking the standing permission in prompt.md line 6.
fs.write to .agent/config.yaml rewrites model, autonomy, tools, network, or credential settings for this and all future runs.
No immutability or provenance tagging protects this store.

evidence.observation: "You may adjust .agent/config.yaml if you need extra tools to finish a task." grants self-modification authority with no approval and no bound on what may be added.
The file controls model, autonomy, max_steps, tools, env (including the PAT), and network for every subsequent run; nothing marks it read-only or provenance-tagged.
Any GitHub user can supply the triggering issue content.

recommendations.action: Make .agent/config.yaml immutable from inside the agent's own runtime; route any legitimate change through a separate, human-reviewed deployment pipeline.
Require a raw_action human approval gate before any self-configuration change takes effect, and remove the prompt's blanket authorization.

findings.title: Confused deputy (TC4): an org-wide, workflow-scoped PAT lets an issue-triggered agent push to and alter CI in any repository in the organization, not only the one it was asked to fix

attack_path.note: Could invoke git/gh CLI with the PAT directly.
Pushes a branch, including a GitHub Actions workflow file, to any repository the org-wide PAT can reach.

findings.residual_rationale: The rubric's write-action sink class treats github.push_branch as S2, but the PAT's workflow scope across every repository in the organization means a single push can add or alter a GitHub Actions workflow file in an unrelated repository, yielding code execution well outside this agent's intended blast radius. That design fact is not captured by the 'write' classification, and the only credited controls cover the shell and the issue input, not the scope of the credential itself, so the floor those credits imply understates the risk.

evidence.observation: Comment states 'repo + workflow scope on all org repos', explicitly exceeding a single repository.
The agent's stated job is to fix issues labeled bug, implying the credential should be scoped to the repository it operates on, not the whole org.

recommendations.action: Issue a short-lived, repo-scoped token without workflow write scope for each task, instead of a standing org-wide PAT.
Add a raw_action human approval gate before any push that touches a .github/workflows path.

findings.title: Forecast: a planned Slack MCP server would add a new untrusted input and egress channel, reopening the lethal trifecta outside the 'issues or code' wording of the current mitigation

forecast.watch_signal: A Slack MCP server entry appears in the MCP client config or tools/list response; check whether Slack content is routed through the same untrusted-input handling as GitHub issues, and whether the server's tool definitions are pinned and identity-verified, before enabling it.

evidence.observation: "The team wants to add a Slack MCP server next quarter." Not yet built, so this path does not exist today.
The only injection defense names 'issues or code' specifically; it was not written with a Slack channel in mind and would need re-verification to cover one.

recommendations.action: Before enabling the Slack MCP server, require definitions_pinned and peer_identity_verified, and treat Slack content as untrusted input routed through the same (or stronger) controls as GitHub issues, rather than an unreviewed addition.

findings.title: No audit trail separates individual agent runs from the shared org-wide PAT identity, undermining accountability for pushes and config changes

attack_path.note: All pushes are authenticated as the single shared PAT identity, not as a distinguishable agent run.

evidence.observation: A single shared PAT authenticates every push and PR; no per-run identity is described in any artifact.
No logging, monitoring, or audit control is mentioned anywhere in the provided artifacts.

recommendations.action: Log every tool call (shell commands, file writes, pushes, config edits) with a run-scoped identifier in an append-only store distinct from the shared PAT identity.

findings.title: Unbounded steps and runtime let an issue-triggered run consume the shared CI runner indefinitely (cost harvesting / denial of service)

attack_path.note: No max_unattended_steps or max_runtime_minutes is enforced (both null).
Runner is shared with other teams' CI, so unbounded consumption is not contained to this agent's own budget.

evidence.observation: max_steps: null, autonomy: full, and no max_runtime_minutes field is present at all.
Runs on a shared CI runner, so unbounded consumption affects other teams' pipelines, not only this agent's own resources.

recommendations.action: Enforce a finite max_unattended_steps and max_runtime_minutes at the orchestrator layer, not only as an absent config value.
Apply a per-run compute/cost cap on the shared CI runner.

rating.rationale: Inherent risk is critical: an unauthenticated GitHub user can label an issue 'bug' and reach an agent that holds an org-wide, workflow-scoped PAT inside an unrestricted-network shell, with full (A4) autonomy and no step or runtime ceiling. Residual stays critical, driven by f.confused_deputy_org_pat: the credential's scope lets a routine code push reach any repository in the organization and add CI workflow files, a design fact the mechanical write-sink classification understates, so it is rated above the floor the two credited behavioral prompt instructions would otherwise produce. The other present findings (secret exfiltration via shell, self-modification of .agent/config.yaml, unbounded resource consumption) each land at high residual: their only mitigations are a 'never exfiltrate' instruction, an 'ignore embedded instructions' instruction, and a self-editable tool list, all dependent controls with no structural backstop (no egress allowlist, no approval gate, no config immutability, no step cap). Forecast remains critical with no further movement needed, but the single control most exposed to decay is con.ignore_embedded_instructions: the model is declared 'latest' and swappable with no review gate, so a model upgrade (or the planned Slack MCP server, which the instruction does not even name) removes the only control standing between untrusted input and the shell/self-config sinks.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in prompt.md, .agent/config.yaml, and the accompanying runtime notes; it does not reflect observed runtime behavior of the deployed agent.

No MCP server config, tool JSON schemas, or orchestration/approval runtime config were provided beyond the two artifacts shown; capability argument validation and whether max_steps or network restrictions are enforced anywhere outside this YAML are inferred, so confidence on some findings (notably f.confused_deputy_org_pat) is medium rather than high.
The planned Slack MCP server is not yet built; f.slack_mcp_forecast is forecast-only per the planned-element rule and should be reassessed once that integration is designed.
